title: Video Doorbells: See Who's at the Door Without Getting Up
subtitle: A plain guide to battery vs. wired models, the monthly fees for saved video, and how to let a family member keep an eye out too.
excerpt: A video doorbell lets you see and talk to whoever is on the porch from your phone, without opening the door. Here is what they cost, which fees to expect for saved video, and how to share access with family.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: The doorbell rings while you are in the middle of lunch, or resting a sore knee, or simply not expecting anyone. Getting up to peek through the curtain is a chore, and opening the door to a stranger is not always wise.

A video doorbell takes care of both problems. AARP's guide to smart home tech notes that doorbell cameras let you see who is at your door without opening it, and many can also alert you when a package arrives. AARP's separate guide to door-to-door scams adds some reassuring advice: you are under no obligation even to answer the doorbell.

The doorbell replaces or sits beside your regular button. It has a small camera, a microphone and a speaker, and it connects to your home Wi-Fi. When someone presses the button or walks up, your phone gets an alert. You can open the app to see a live picture and talk through the doorbell, all from your chair.
The two big choices are how it gets power and where it keeps recorded video. Live view is generally included. Saving and replaying clips later is where monthly fees often come in.

Battery models are the easiest to put up, since they do not need doorbell wiring. The trade-off is recharging. Ring's Battery Doorbell 2K, for example, has a battery you take off the mount to charge, though it can also trickle-charge from existing doorbell wires. Wired models draw power from the low-voltage wires your old doorbell already uses, so there is nothing to recharge, but installation takes a little more confidence or a helper.

Most brands store clips in the cloud for a monthly or yearly fee. A few, like eufy, keep video on the doorbell itself so there is no required subscription. If you mostly want to see who is there right now, you may not need a plan at all. If you want to look back at what happened while you were out, budget for one.

items: The yearly cost, not just the sticker price. Add the plan fee you would actually pay over two or three years.
Battery or wired. Battery is simpler to install; wired means no recharging. Some battery models can be wired later.
Your indoor chime. Check whether the doorbell works with the chime you already have, or whether you need to buy one, so you can hear it from the back bedroom.
A simple app. Large buttons and a clear live-view screen matter more than a long feature list.
Family sharing. Look for a way to invite a son, daughter or neighbor to see the doorbell from their own phone, with limits you choose.
Your Wi-Fi. Several models work only on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, and the signal needs to reach the front door.

sections.content: This is where a video doorbell can help a whole family. In the Ring app, the account owner can add a Shared User by email and choose which devices that person can see. Google's Home app lets you invite a household member as either an Admin or a Member; by default, Members can see live camera view, and you can separately turn on access to camera history.

A practical setup: the parent who lives in the home stays the owner, and a grown child is added with view access so they can check in, or answer the door by voice if a delivery driver needs directions.
Setting it up and keeping it private
Many doorbells are do-it-yourself jobs. Ring says its battery model takes about 10 minutes. If ladders or wiring are not your thing, this is a good afternoon project to do with a family member.
The Federal Trade Commission's advice on securing home cameras boils down to a few habits worth following:

items: Use a strong password you have never used anywhere else, and turn on two-factor sign-in if offered.
Protect your home Wi-Fi with a strong password and keep the router updated.
Turn on automatic updates for the doorbell and its app.
Limit who can change settings, and only share the live view with people you trust.

sections.label: Good to Know
sections.content: Without a plan, most doorbells still let you see and talk to a visitor live. Google's Nest Doorbell (battery) includes three hours of event video history at no charge, and the eufy E340 saves clips on 8 GB of built-in storage with no subscription required. A paid plan mainly buys you longer video history and extra alerts.

A video doorbell will not answer the door for you, but it lets you decide whether to answer at all, from wherever you are sitting. Pick one that fits your budget for the long run, share it with someone you trust, and remember the simple rule from AARP: when in doubt, keep strangers out.

products.name: Battery Doorbell 2K
products.price: About $44.99 on sale (list $99.99, October 2026); saved-video plans from $4.99 a month
products.blurb: A good fit for renters or anyone who wants a no-wiring install: removable rechargeable battery, head-to-toe view, two-way talk, and it works with existing mechanical and digital chimes. Plans offer up to 180 days of video history.

products.name: Nest Doorbell (battery)
products.price: About $199.99 (Google Store, October 2026); saved-video plans from $10 a month
products.blurb: Suits families already using Google Home or a Nest display. It includes three hours of event video history without a subscription, alerts that tell you when a person is at the door, and keeps recording for an hour if the Wi-Fi drops.

products.name: Video Doorbell E340 (Battery Powered)
products.blurb: For people who would rather skip monthly fees: video is saved on 8 GB of built-in storage. Dual cameras show the doormat for packages, it runs on battery or doorbell wiring, and it works with an existing mechanical chime.
